title: Working with APIs
tagline: Call web APIs, connect services together, and reach into C libraries from Python
description: How programs talk to other programs, in Python: HTTP requests and JSON, reading an API's documentation, API keys, tokens and OAuth with PKCE, signed requests, paging, rate limits, retries with backoff, idempotency and caching, receiving and verifying webhooks, joining two services together with mapping, incremental sync and failure handling, and finally calling C libraries with ctypes. The practice uses small fake servers, so every task runs anywhere and every edge case can be tested; each milestone ends with five projects, from small to large. It assumes the Python course.

milestones.title: HTTP and JSON
milestones.blurb: What a web API is, requests and responses, JSON in Python, reading an API's reference, and building URLs and clients that do not break on unusual input.

lessons.title: What a Web API Is
lessons.summary: Programs talking to programs - what an API is, how web APIs use HTTP, resources and endpoints in the REST style, the other styles you will meet (GraphQL, RPC, WebSockets), and what calling one from Python looks like with urllib and requests.

lessons.title: Requests and Responses
lessons.summary: The parts of an HTTP request and response as an API client sees them - method, URL with path and query, headers such as Content-Type, Accept and Authorization, the body, status codes and their families, response headers worth reading, and timeouts.

lessons.title: JSON in Python
lessons.summary: The JSON format and how Python's json module maps it to dicts, lists, strings, numbers, True, False and None - parsing and producing text, what happens with errors, numbers and Unicode, and checking that a document from an API has the shape your code expects.

lessons.title: Reading an API Reference
lessons.summary: Getting everything you need from a web API's documentation - base URL and versions, the endpoint list, path and query parameters, request and response bodies, error codes, authentication and limits - and the OpenAPI description many APIs publish, which you can read and even generate clients from.

tasks.title: A request from an endpoint description

lessons.title: Building URLs and Clients Safely
lessons.summary: Building requests that do not break on unusual input - escaping path segments and query values with urllib.parse, why string concatenation goes wrong, lists and booleans in query strings - and structuring a small API client around an injectable transport with one place for errors.

milestones.title: Keys and Sign-in
milestones.blurb: API keys and where secrets belong, bearer tokens that expire, OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, signing requests with HMAC, and keeping secrets out of logs.

lessons.title: API Keys and Where Secrets Belong
lessons.summary: The simplest way APIs identify a caller - the API key - how to send it, why never in the URL, where secrets live (environment variables, untracked files, secret managers, never in code), keeping keys narrow in what they can do, and what to do the day one leaks.

lessons.title: Bearer Tokens and Expiry
lessons.summary: Access tokens that expire - the Authorization Bearer header, expires_in and computing when to renew with a safety margin, refresh tokens, retrying once after a 401, caching a token across calls, and what a JWT is and why a client should not trust what it reads in one.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0 and PKCE
lessons.summary: Acting on behalf of a user without ever seeing their password - the OAuth 2.0 roles, the authorization code flow step by step with PKCE and the state parameter, scopes and redirect URIs, the client credentials flow for server-to-server calls, and why you use a well-tested library.

lessons.title: Signing Requests with HMAC
lessons.summary: Proving a request came from you and was not changed - HMAC with a shared secret, building a canonical string from the method, path, sorted query, timestamp and body hash, why every byte must be agreed, timestamps against replay, and comparing signatures in constant time.

lessons.title: Keeping Secrets Out of Logs
lessons.summary: The many quiet ways secrets leak - URLs, headers and bodies in logs, error messages, tracebacks, object reprs and debugging output - and how to redact them systematically, from masking a key for display to scrubbing nested JSON, plus a test that proves no secret reaches the log.

milestones.title: Paging, Rate Limits and Retries
milestones.blurb: Offset, page and cursor pagination, rate limits and Retry-After, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, idempotency keys, and caching with ETags.

lessons.title: Pagination
lessons.summary: Getting long lists from an API one page at a time - offset and limit, page numbers, cursors and Link headers - how each behaves when data changes while you read, loop protection, and Python generators that make paging invisible to the rest of your code.

lessons.title: Rate Limits
lessons.summary: How APIs limit how fast you call them - per-second, per-minute and daily limits, the 429 status, Retry-After in seconds or as a date, rate-limit headers - and staying under the limit on your side with a token bucket instead of waiting to be told off.

lessons.title: Retries with Backoff
lessons.summary: Recovering from the failures that go away by themselves - which errors and statuses are worth retrying, why only idempotent requests are safe to repeat, exponential backoff with a cap, full jitter, honouring Retry-After, and limiting attempts and total time.

lessons.title: Idempotency Keys and Timeouts
lessons.summary: Making non-idempotent requests safe to retry - the Idempotency-Key header, one key per logical operation, what the server stores and replays, conflicts when the same key comes with a different request - and timeouts, unknown outcomes and deadlines that span several calls.

tasks.title: Idempotency keys on the server side

lessons.title: Caching with ETags
lessons.summary: Not asking for what you already have - HTTP caching headers as an API client uses them, Cache-Control max-age and no-store, ETags with If-None-Match and the 304 Not Modified answer, Last-Modified, and a small client-side cache that saves requests and rate limit.

milestones.title: Webhooks
milestones.blurb: Webhooks versus polling, verifying signatures, handling retried, duplicated and out-of-order deliveries, a receiver from raw HTTP, and testing webhooks.

lessons.title: Webhooks versus Polling
lessons.summary: Two ways to learn that something changed at another service - asking repeatedly (polling) and being told (webhooks) - what each costs, polling done carefully with an updated-since cursor and adaptive intervals, and how webhook subscriptions, events and deliveries work.

lessons.title: Verifying Webhook Signatures
lessons.summary: Making sure a webhook really came from the service - why a public endpoint must verify every request, the common signature scheme of timestamp plus HMAC of the raw body, signature headers with several values during secret rotation, tolerance windows, and the mistakes that break verification.

lessons.title: Handling Deliveries
lessons.summary: What a webhook endpoint must assume about deliveries - they are retried, so they arrive more than once; they arrive out of order; and they must be answered quickly - and the techniques that cope - acknowledge fast and queue, idempotent processing by event id with bounded memory, and versions or fetching current state for ordering.

lessons.title: A Webhook Receiver
lessons.summary: The HTTP side of a webhook endpoint - what a raw request looks like on the wire, parsing the request line, headers and body by Content-Length, choosing status codes for every failure, a minimal receiver with Python's http.server, and what production adds (a framework, HTTPS, a queue).

lessons.title: Testing Webhooks
lessons.summary: Testing the code that receives webhooks without waiting for real events - fixture deliveries built and signed in tests, testing every rejection path, replaying recorded deliveries, the service's own test events and CLI tools, and exposing a local endpoint with a tunnel during development.

milestones.title: Joining Services Together
milestones.blurb: Designing an integration, mapping data between two APIs, incremental sync with checkpoints and deletes, partial failure and dead letters, and keeping an integration observable.

lessons.title: Designing an Integration
lessons.summary: The decisions to make before writing code that connects two services - which system owns which data, one-way or two-way, triggered by webhooks, schedules or users, how records in one system find their partners in the other, and writing it all down on one page.

lessons.title: Mapping Data Between APIs
lessons.summary: Turning one API's records into another's - a field mapping table, money as integers or decimals rather than floats, enumerations mapped explicitly with a decision for unknown values, names and emails, missing versus null, and dates and times across time zones with ISO 8601, datetime and zoneinfo.

tasks.title: Mapping an order to an invoice

lessons.title: Incremental Sync
lessons.summary: Copying only what changed since last time - checkpoints and updated-since queries, upserting by external id so that reruns are safe, deletes through tombstones or periodic reconciliation, the first run over existing data, and the extra problems of two-way sync - conflicts and echo loops.

lessons.title: Partial Failure and Dead Letters
lessons.summary: What to do when some records fail and others succeed - never letting one bad record stop the rest, sorting failures into transient and permanent, retrying the transient ones, keeping the permanent ones in a dead-letter list with the reason, replaying them after a fix, and the outbox pattern for keeping a database and an API in step.

lessons.title: Keeping an Integration Observable
lessons.summary: Knowing an integration works without watching it - structured log lines with correlation ids, a summary per run, the few numbers worth tracking (processed, failed, dead letters, lag), alerts that fire on the right things, health checks, and scheduling runs with cron or Windows Task Scheduler.

tasks.title: Structured logs and a run summary

milestones.title: Calling C Libraries
milestones.blurb: Why and how Python calls C, ctypes types and function signatures, structures, pointers and buffers, callbacks and errors, and the other ways languages bind to C.

lessons.title: Why Python Calls C
lessons.summary: The other kind of API - a native library's functions - why C's calling convention is the common language every other language can speak, what you gain by calling into C from Python, the tools available (ctypes, cffi, extension modules), and the new kind of failure it brings - crashes instead of exceptions.

lessons.title: ctypes Basics
lessons.summary: Calling a C function from Python with ctypes - loading a library on Windows, Linux and macOS, the ctypes types that match C types, why argtypes and restype must always be set, how ints, bytes, str and None are passed, and translating a function's declaration from its header line by line.

lessons.title: Structures, Pointers and Buffers
lessons.summary: Passing data rather than single values - ctypes Structure and the C rules for field alignment and padding, packed structures, arrays, passing by reference with byref and pointer, buffers created with create_string_buffer, and the question that decides crashes - who owns and frees each piece of memory.

lessons.title: Callbacks and Errors
lessons.summary: When C calls back into Python - CFUNCTYPE and WINFUNCTYPE, keeping callbacks alive, exceptions inside callbacks - and how C reports errors - return codes, errno with use_errno, GetLastError with use_last_error and WinError, and errcheck to turn return codes into Python exceptions automatically.

lessons.title: Other Ways to Bind C
lessons.summary: Beyond ctypes - cffi working from C declarations, extension modules and pybind11 for speed and C++, generating bindings from headers - and how other languages call the same C API - C# P/Invoke, JavaScript through N-API and FFI packages, Rust's extern blocks and bindgen - and how to choose.
